q: The two main hormones secreted by the human ovaries are:
x: The ovaries secrete oestrogen (mainly from the follicle) and progesterone (mainly from the corpus luteum). FSH and LH come from the anterior pituitary.

q: Which of these is a function of the vagina?
o: It receives sperm during intercourse and forms the birth canal
It is the site of fertilisation
x: The vagina receives the penis and sperm and acts as the birth canal. Ova are made in the ovaries and fertilisation occurs in the oviduct.

q: Compared with a sperm, a human ovum is:
o: Smaller and moves by a flagellum
Of the same size but has no nucleus
Much larger and non-motile, with stored food
Larger and moves by many cilia
x: The ovum is a large, non-motile cell with stored nutrients in its cytoplasm. The sperm is tiny and swims using its tail (flagellum).

q: Inhibin, which reduces the secretion of FSH in the male, is produced by the:
x: Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which acts on the anterior pituitary to lower FSH. Leydig cells secrete testosterone.

q: Semen is slightly alkaline. This helps the sperm mainly because it:
o: Neutralises the acidity of the vagina
Supplies fructose as an energy source
Keeps the sperm still until ejaculation
x: The vagina is acidic, which harms sperm; the alkaline secretions in semen neutralise this acid. Fructose for energy comes from the seminal vesicles, but that is a separate function from alkalinity.

q: Which male gland contributes the largest share of the volume of semen?
x: The seminal vesicles supply most of the fluid volume of semen (roughly 60%). The testes provide the sperm but only a small part of the volume.

q: Erection of the penis occurs when:
o: Its spongy erectile tissue fills with blood
Its muscles contract around a bone
The testes rise into the abdomen
x: The penis contains spongy erectile tissue. When its arteries dilate, blood fills these spaces and the penis becomes firm. Humans have no bone in the penis.

q: The acrosome at the tip of the sperm head contains:
o: Mitochondria that supply energy for swimming
Enzymes that help the sperm pass through the layers around the oocyte
The centrioles that form the tail
x: The acrosome is a cap of digestive enzymes, such as hyaluronidase, released to break through the coverings of the oocyte. Mitochondria lie in the middle piece.

q: The middle piece of a human sperm is packed with mitochondria. Their role is to:
o: Digest the coverings of the oocyte
Supply ATP for the beating of the tail
Store food for the developing embryo
x: Mitochondria in the middle piece produce ATP, which powers the movement of the flagellum. The chromosomes are in the head and the enzymes in the acrosome.

q: The thick muscular layer of the uterine wall that contracts strongly during childbirth is the:
x: The myometrium is the smooth muscle layer of the uterus. The endometrium is the inner lining that thickens each cycle and receives the embryo.

q: Strong contractions of the uterus during childbirth are stimulated by:
x: Oxytocin, released from the posterior pituitary, causes the myometrium to contract during labour. Progesterone does the opposite during pregnancy and keeps the uterus quiet.

q: After childbirth, the production of milk by the mammary glands is stimulated mainly by:
x: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production. Oxytocin causes the milk to be ejected (let down) during suckling.

q: Spermatogonia, which lie next to the wall of the seminiferous tubule, increase in number by:
x: Spermatogonia are diploid stem cells that multiply by mitosis. Some then grow into primary spermatocytes, which enter meiosis.

q: How many chromosomes does a human spermatid contain?
x: Spermatids are formed by meiosis II, so they are haploid with 23 chromosomes (22 autosomes and one sex chromosome).

q: If 25 primary spermatocytes and 25 primary oocytes all complete meiosis, how many functional gametes are formed?
x: Each primary spermatocyte gives four sperm (25 × 4 = 100). Each primary oocyte gives only one functional ovum, the other products being polar bodies.

q: In oogenesis, the first polar body is formed at the end of:
x: Meiosis I in the primary oocyte divides the cytoplasm unequally, giving a large secondary oocyte and a small first polar body.

q: In a vasectomy, a small part of each vas deferens is cut and tied. Which result is expected?
o: Semen contains no sperm, but testosterone secretion continues normally
Testosterone secretion stops, so male features are lost
No semen at all is produced
Sperm production in the testes stops completely
x: Cutting the vas deferens blocks the passage of sperm, so the ejaculate lacks sperm. The Leydig cells and the glands that make seminal fluid are not affected.

q: In tubal ligation, both oviducts of a woman are cut and tied. This prevents pregnancy because:
o: The uterus can no longer shed its lining
Sperm and oocyte can no longer meet in the oviduct
x: Fertilisation normally happens in the oviduct. With both tubes blocked, sperm cannot reach the oocyte. The ovaries and the cycle continue to work.

q: A man takes large doses of synthetic testosterone-like steroids for body-building. His testes are likely to:
o: Enlarge and produce more sperm, because testosterone is high
Shrink and produce fewer sperm, because FSH and LH are suppressed
Stay unchanged, because steroids act only on muscles
Begin secreting oestrogen instead of testosterone
x: High steroid levels feed back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering GnRH, FSH and LH. Without these, the testes shrink and sperm production falls.

q: Normal spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules needs:
x: FSH acts on the Sertoli cells and testosterone from the Leydig cells acts within the tubules; both are required for full sperm production.

q: Testosterone, oestrogen and progesterone all belong to which chemical class of hormones?
x: The sex hormones are steroids made from cholesterol. FSH and LH, by contrast, are glycoproteins.

q: About how many oocytes are released by ovulation during a woman's entire reproductive life?
x: Although the ovaries contain hundreds of thousands of oocytes at puberty, usually only one is released each cycle, giving roughly 400 over the reproductive years.

q: In the human female, the urethra:
o: Joins the vagina and carries urine and ova
Opens separately from the vagina and carries only urine
Carries both urine and menstrual fluid
x: In the female, the urinary and reproductive openings are separate. In the male, the urethra carries both urine and semen.

q: The first menstruation in a girl's life, at puberty, is called:
x: Menarche is the first menstrual period, usually at about 10 to 14 years of age. Menopause is the permanent end of the cycles.

q: Menstrual bleeding usually lasts about:
x: The menstrual phase normally lasts about 3 to 5 days, at the start of the cycle.

q: The main purpose of the monthly changes in the uterus is to:
o: Prepare the endometrium to receive an embryo
x: Each cycle the endometrium is built up so that a fertilised egg could implant. If no pregnancy occurs, it is shed and the cycle starts again.

q: Normally, how many follicles complete development and release an oocyte in each menstrual cycle?
x: Several follicles begin to grow, but usually only one becomes a mature (Graafian) follicle and ovulates; the rest degenerate.

q: Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) in early pregnancy is secreted by the:
o: Developing embryo (its chorion, which forms part of the placenta)
x: hCG is made by the chorion of the early embryo. It keeps the corpus luteum alive so that progesterone stays high.

q: A home pregnancy test works by detecting which hormone in a woman's urine?
x: Pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotrophin, which is made only by the embryo and placenta, so its presence indicates pregnancy.

q: Menopause, the end of menstrual cycles at about 45 to 55 years of age, occurs because:
o: The ovaries stop responding to FSH and LH, so oestrogen and progesterone fall
The pituitary stops making FSH and LH
The uterus is removed by the body
x: At menopause the ovaries run out of responsive follicles, so oestrogen and progesterone fall. With less negative feedback, FSH and LH actually rise.

q: The white scar-like tissue left in the ovary after the corpus luteum degenerates is the:
x: When the corpus luteum breaks down it is replaced by fibrous tissue called the corpus albicans ('white body').

q: A woman's resting body temperature rises slightly soon after ovulation and stays higher until menstruation. This rise is caused by:
x: Progesterone, secreted during the luteal phase, raises the basal body temperature by a few tenths of a degree. It falls again when the corpus luteum degenerates.

q: Near ovulation, the cervical mucus becomes thin and watery, making it easier for sperm to pass. This change is caused by:
x: Rising oestrogen before ovulation makes cervical mucus thin and stretchy. After ovulation, progesterone makes it thick again.

q: The level of oestrogen in the blood reaches its highest peak:
o: At the end of the luteal phase
Immediately after the corpus luteum degenerates
x: The large Graafian follicle secretes a peak of oestrogen in the days just before ovulation. This peak triggers the LH surge.

q: At mid-cycle, which pituitary hormones show a sharp peak at the same time?
x: Both LH and FSH rise sharply at mid-cycle, LH much more than FSH. Oestrogen and progesterone are ovarian, not pituitary, hormones.

q: During the follicular phase, which ovarian hormone remains at a low level?
x: Progesterone stays low until the corpus luteum forms after ovulation. Oestrogen rises steadily during the follicular phase.

q: In a regular 28-day cycle, the proliferative phase of the uterus lasts roughly from:
x: Days 1–5 are menstruation; the endometrium then rebuilds (proliferative phase) until ovulation at about day 14. The secretory phase follows.

q: The corpus luteum is kept active during the luteal phase of a cycle by:
x: LH forms and supports the corpus luteum. As progesterone suppresses LH, support fades and the corpus luteum breaks down unless hCG from an embryo takes over.

q: Throughout pregnancy, progesterone helps to:
o: Cause the endometrium to be shed
Keep the uterine muscle relaxed so the embryo is not expelled
x: Progesterone maintains the endometrium and reduces contractions of the myometrium. A fall in its level is one factor in starting menstruation or labour.

q: After about the first three months of pregnancy, most of the progesterone is produced by the:
x: The corpus luteum maintains progesterone early in pregnancy; later the placenta takes over this role and the corpus luteum declines.

q: When progesterone falls at the end of a cycle, the coiled (spiral) arteries of the endometrium:
o: Grow longer to support an embryo
Constrict, cutting the blood supply so the lining breaks down
x: Without progesterone, the spiral arteries constrict and the outer endometrium dies and is shed with blood as menstruation.

q: If the LH surge fails to occur in a cycle, which result is expected?
o: No ovulation, and so no corpus luteum forms
The corpus luteum persists for months
x: The LH surge is the trigger for ovulation and for turning the follicle into a corpus luteum. Without it, the follicle does not release its oocyte.

q: The luteal phase lasts about 14 days in most women. A woman has regular 32-day cycles. Ovulation is expected on about:
x: Ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next period: 32 − 14 = 18. The follicular phase varies, so day 14 applies only to 28-day cycles.

q: Both ovaries of a 30-year-old woman are surgically removed. Which change is expected?
o: Her cycles continue, with normal FSH and LH
Her cycles stop, and FSH and LH levels fall
Her cycles stop, and FSH and LH levels rise
Her progesterone rises, and FSH and LH fall
x: Without ovaries, no oestrogen or progesterone is made, so the endometrium is no longer built up. With no negative feedback, the pituitary releases more FSH and LH.

q: A blood test on day 3 of a woman's cycle shows low progesterone, low oestrogen and slowly rising FSH. Which stage does this match?
x: Early in the cycle, the corpus luteum has gone, so both ovarian hormones are low and FSH rises to start new follicles growing. Before ovulation oestrogen would be high; in the luteal phase or pregnancy progesterone would be high.

q: Non-identical (fraternal) twins develop when:
o: One fertilised egg splits into two embryos
One oocyte is fertilised by two sperm
Two follicles release oocytes in the same cycle and each is fertilised by a different sperm
One follicle releases one oocyte that divides before fertilisation
x: Fraternal twins come from two separate oocytes and two sperm, so they are as alike as ordinary siblings. A single zygote that splits gives identical twins.

q: The full form of AIDS is:
x: AIDS stands for Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome, the late stage of infection with HIV, the human immunodeficiency virus.

q: Besides sexual contact, HIV is commonly spread by:
o: Shaking hands with an infected person
Sharing needles and transfusion of unscreened blood
x: HIV spreads through blood, semen, vaginal fluid and breast milk, so shared needles and unscreened blood are major routes. Casual contact does not spread it.

q: HIV is classified as a retrovirus because it:
o: Has DNA and makes RNA from it
Has RNA and makes DNA from it by reverse transcriptase
Has no nucleic acid at all
x: Retroviruses carry RNA and use reverse transcriptase to copy it into DNA, the reverse of the usual DNA-to-RNA flow.

q: HIV recognises and enters helper T cells by binding to which surface protein?
x: The HIV envelope glycoprotein attaches to the CD4 receptor on helper T cells (and some other cells), so these are its main targets.

q: Inside a helper T cell, the DNA copy of the HIV genome:
o: Is broken down immediately by the host
Is inserted into the host cell's own DNA
Is released from the cell as free DNA
Is converted into protein without transcription
x: Viral DNA made by reverse transcriptase is integrated into the host chromosome as a provirus. It can stay hidden for years and later direct new virus production.

q: HIV is NOT spread by:
o: Unprotected sex with an infected person
Sharing razors used by an infected person
x: Mosquitoes do not transmit HIV; the virus does not multiply in them. Sex, shared razors and breast milk can all carry infected body fluids.

q: Shortly after HIV infection, many people have:
o: Immediate collapse of the immune system
A rash only on the palms and soles
A short flu-like illness with fever and swollen lymph nodes
x: The early stage often causes a brief flu-like illness. Years usually pass before the immune system fails and AIDS develops.

q: Which infection is common in people with AIDS but rare in healthy people?
x: Pneumocystis pneumonia is a typical opportunistic infection in AIDS; it rarely causes illness when the immune system is normal. Tuberculosis is also common in AIDS.

q: A person infected with HIV two weeks ago gives a negative result on an HIV antibody test. The most likely reason is that:
o: HIV is destroyed within two weeks
HIV is never found in blood
Antibodies against HIV have not yet been made in detectable amounts
x: It takes some weeks for the body to make enough antibodies to be detected; this gap is the window period. During it, the person can still pass on the virus.

q: Which of the following helps to prevent the spread of HIV in hospitals and clinics?
o: Using sterile, disposable syringes and screened blood
x: HIV is carried in blood, so single-use sterile syringes and screening of blood for transfusion stop its spread. Antibiotics do not act on viruses.

q: Antibiotics such as penicillin cure syphilis but have no effect on genital herpes or HIV. The reason is that:
o: Viruses lack the bacterial structures, such as cell walls and 70S ribosomes, that antibiotics attack
Herpes and HIV live only outside cells
Antibiotics are destroyed by the immune system
x: Antibiotics target features of bacteria, such as cell-wall synthesis or 70S ribosomes. Viruses have none of these and multiply inside host cells.

q: Symptoms of gonorrhoea in an infected man usually appear:
o: Within about a week of infection
Only after the person reaches old age
x: Gonorrhoea has a short incubation period; symptoms such as painful urination and discharge usually appear within a few days to a week.

q: If gonorrhoea is not treated in a man, the infection can spread to the epididymis and cause:
x: Spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae to the epididymis can cause inflammation and scarring that blocks sperm passage, leading to sterility.

q: When gonorrhoea causes symptoms in a woman, they may include:
o: A rash on the palms and soles
Vaginal discharge and pain on passing urine
x: Women with gonorrhoea may have a vaginal discharge and painful urination, though many have no symptoms. A painless ulcer suggests syphilis; blisters suggest herpes.

q: Four days after sexual exposure, a man has painful urination with a thick yellow discharge. Pus from the urethra shows Gram-negative diplococci. The disease is:
x: Gram-negative diplococci in urethral pus with painful discharge soon after exposure point to Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Syphilis is caused by a spiral bacterium and herpes by a virus.

q: The soft, destructive, tumour-like lesions that may appear in the skin, bones or organs in tertiary syphilis are called:
x: Gummas are typical of tertiary syphilis. A chancre is the painless ulcer of the primary stage, and vesicles are the blisters of herpes.

q: Which statement about the two types of herpes simplex virus is correct?
o: HSV-2 mainly causes genital herpes, while HSV-1 mainly causes cold sores around the mouth
HSV-1 causes syphilis, while HSV-2 causes gonorrhoea
Both types cause only skin rashes on the palms
x: HSV-2 is the usual cause of genital herpes and HSV-1 of oral cold sores, though each can infect either site.

q: A patient with repeated outbreaks of genital herpes is prescribed acyclovir. What can this antiviral drug achieve?
o: Complete removal of the virus after a single dose
Fewer and shorter outbreaks, though the virus stays in the body
Permanent immunity against all sexually transmitted diseases
Killing the bacteria that cause the blisters
x: Antiviral drugs such as acyclovir shorten and reduce outbreaks, but the virus stays latent in nerve cells for life. Penicillin acts only on bacteria.

q: A pregnant woman has active genital herpes sores at the time of delivery. The main risk is that:
o: The baby may be infected during birth and become seriously ill
The baby will be born with syphilis
The baby will be born with sickle-cell anaemia
The mother will become sterile immediately
x: Herpes can pass to the baby during passage through the birth canal, and newborn herpes can be severe. Doctors may advise a caesarean delivery in such cases.

q: Which pairing of a sexually transmitted disease with the type of its causative agent is correct?
x: Genital herpes and AIDS are caused by viruses (HSV and HIV). Gonorrhoea and syphilis are caused by bacteria.

q: In an outbreak of genital herpes, the typical sequence of the skin lesions is:
o: Small blisters form, burst into painful ulcers, then crust and heal
A painless hard ulcer forms and lasts for years
A rash on the palms spreads to the whole body
Warts grow slowly and never heal
x: Herpes blisters (vesicles) rupture to leave painful shallow ulcers that crust over and heal in one to two weeks; the virus then becomes latent.

q: The causative agent of AIDS is:
x: AIDS is caused by HIV, the human immunodeficiency virus. Herpes simplex causes genital herpes, Treponema causes syphilis and Neisseria causes gonorrhoea.
